title: Security
one_line_goal: Blocking, permissions and isolation proven by tests; threat model written
summary: Build the security rules engine and prove with attack-style tests what Ferrum protects and what it does not. The cost of security is only designed here; it is measured in P6.

tasks.title: Threat model
tasks.what: A threat model: what we protect, who might attack, where trust changes, and which threats are in or out of scope. The security document is completed.
tasks.why: Without a threat model, security work is guesswork: some risks get several defences and others none, and nobody can say which risks are left open.
tasks.how: Start from the part pages, which mark where trust changes; for each place, list who could attack (a bad site, a bad frame, a bad library, a local program) and what defends it.
tasks.chain: Controls need a reason → list what we protect, who attacks and where trust changes, and map each threat to a control and test, or 'not enforced' → every later task traces to a threat.
tasks.check: The security document maps every boundary and threat to a control and a test, or says not enforced.

tasks.title: Rules engine
tasks.what: A rules engine that decides if a navigation is allowed, with block and allow lists and a reason for every decision.
tasks.why: If each feature made its own allow or block choice, the choices would drift apart and gaps would open. One place makes every decision checkable and explainable.
tasks.how: Plain Rust code: HTTPS allowed, plain HTTP upgraded or warned, other link types need confirmation. A more specific allow beats a block. Tests cover every branch.
tasks.chain: Navigation needs one decision point → plain Rust rules: block and allow lists, HTTPS upgrade, ask for other link types, deny anything unreadable → safe by default, every decision explained.
tasks.check: Tests per rule plus random inputs; every decision branch covered (report saved).

tasks.title: Check every navigation path
tasks.what: Checks on every way a page can move: direct links, redirects, embedded frames, pop-ups and malformed addresses.
tasks.why: A rule that only some paths check is easy to get around: a blocked site could still load through a redirect, a frame or a pop-up.
tasks.how: Also hook WebView2's own navigation, frame and new-window events, and re-check every redirect step. Tests try each bypass and expect a denial and a log line.
tasks.chain: Tauri's hook misses unreadable addresses and embedded frames → also hook WebView2's own events and re-check each redirect → no way around the rules by redirect, frame or pop-up.
tasks.check: A blocked site is denied and logged via direct link, redirect, frame, pop-up and malformed address.

tasks.title: Ask before opening other apps
tasks.what: Links that would open another program on your PC first ask you.
tasks.why: Without this, a website could launch a program on your computer without asking, which attackers use to run their own code.
tasks.how: Catch WebView2's external-link event, ask for confirmation in the shell, and keep an allowlist per link type. A test proves nothing launches without consent.
tasks.chain: Links can launch other programs → confirm in the shell, with an allowlist per link type → nothing launches silently.
tasks.check: Without consent the other program is never started.

tasks.title: Permission prompts
tasks.what: Ferrum, not WebView2, decides on camera, microphone, location, notifications and clipboard reading.
tasks.why: A website with silent camera, microphone or location access could spy on you. Decisions stored inside WebView2 would be out of your sight and control.
tasks.how: Send permission requests to the rules engine, keep per-site grants in settings, and tell WebView2 not to save decisions itself. Tests check deny, grant and revoke.
tasks.chain: Camera, microphone, location, notifications and clipboard are sensitive → deny by default, allow per site, never stored inside WebView2 → you control access.
tasks.check: Each kind is denied by default; a grant works and can be revoked.

tasks.title: Safe downloads
tasks.what: Safer downloads: only into the set folder, never opened automatically, a warning for program files, cleaned file names.
tasks.why: A download named to look harmless could be saved outside the folder or start a program by itself. That is a common way to infect a computer.
tasks.how: Save files only into the set folder, strip unsafe parts from each file name, never open a file by itself, and warn on program types. Whether Windows marks downloads as unsafe is not checked yet.
tasks.chain: Downloads can hide tricks → configured folder only, no auto-open, a warning for programs, cleaned file names → no folder-escape tricks.
tasks.check: Trick names and program files land cleaned in the folder, with a warning.

tasks.title: Prove what is really isolated
tasks.what: Settings for per-site profiles, optional private tabs and clearing one profile, plus a tested list of what profiles still share.
tasks.why: Saying 'each site is fully separate' without proof would mislead you and the paper's readers, because profiles still share some browser processes.
tasks.how: Configure the profile, private-tab and clearing settings, then look at which processes and files each profile really uses, instead of trusting the documentation.
tasks.chain: Profiles share browser processes → test what is truly separate (cookies, storage, databases) and list what is shared → no claim of full isolation without evidence.
tasks.check: Site A's data is unreadable from B; clearing A leaves B intact; the shared list cites evidence.

tasks.title: No app access for websites
tasks.what: Websites cannot reach any app command, built-in command, app message channel or the app's own pages.
tasks.why: If one channel were left open, any website could control Ferrum and, through it, your files. The bridge is present in every view, so only checks keep it shut.
tasks.how: From a remote test page, try every path, including one internal command the permission system skips, and a jump to the app's own pages. All must fail.
tasks.chain: Websites must not reach app internals → test every channel, including one internal command the permission system skips, and block loading the app's own pages → native access stays closed.
tasks.check: Every listed path fails from a remote test page.

tasks.title: Security audit log
tasks.what: A security log with one line per blocked action: time, tab, site, action, rule and decision.
tasks.why: Without a record you cannot tell whether a block happened or why. Storing page content would turn the log itself into a privacy risk.
tasks.how: Write lines to a log file that is rolled over when it grows. Each security test checks its log line exists, and a format test checks every line.
tasks.chain: Denials need a record → one log line per denied action, old logs rolled over, with no page content → evidence without privacy leaks.
tasks.check: Each security test finds its record; all records match the format.

tasks.title: Recover from crashes
tasks.what: Recovery when a tab's page process or the browser process crashes.
tasks.why: Without recovery, one crashing website could take every other tab and the whole window down with it.
tasks.how: Listen to WebView2's crash and exit events and show a crashed tab with a reload option. A test crashes a tab on purpose, using a method from a P1 experiment, then reloads it.
tasks.chain: Page processes crash → show a crashed tab, allow reload, keep the shell alive → one bad site cannot take Ferrum down.
tasks.check: A deliberate crash shows the crashed state; reload works; the shell stays responsive.

tasks.title: One security test suite
tasks.what: One security test suite covering all ten security tests your brief asks for.
tasks.why: Scattered tests make it hard to see whether all ten security items are covered. Mixing them with speed tests could hide a security failure.
tasks.how: One command runs the suite, including the allowlist cases. A table on the security page maps each of the ten items to its test.
tasks.chain: Your brief lists ten security tests → one suite mapping each to a test, kept apart from speed tests → coverage is visible.
tasks.check: The suite passes, including allowlist cases; the mapping table is published.

tasks.title: Selectable isolation modes
tasks.what: Three isolation modes you can pick in settings: everything shared, a profile per site, or a separate data folder per site.
tasks.why: Stronger isolation costs memory and processes. Without all three modes working, P6 could not measure that cost, and you could not choose your balance.
tasks.how: Add a setting that picks the mode at start: all tabs in one profile, one profile per site, or one data folder per site. Then observe what each mode really shares.
tasks.chain: Isolation has a cost → three modes set in config (shared, a profile per site, a data folder per site), observed rather than assumed → P6 can compare them.
tasks.check: The same two-site test per mode shows the expected separation; process counts recorded; any mode that fails is recorded with its error.

tasks.title: Benchmark-only 'no security' switch
tasks.what: A build-time switch that turns all security rules off, for benchmarks on local test pages only.
tasks.why: Without a version that has no security, its cost cannot be measured. If that version were ever shipped, every protection would be gone.
tasks.how: Add a compile-time option that makes every rule answer 'allow', keep it out of release builds, and require a benchmark-only start argument to run it.
tasks.chain: Measuring security's cost needs a version without it → a build-time switch for local test pages only, proven absent from release builds → no risk of shipping it.
tasks.check: With the switch everything is allowed; the release build is scanned and the switch is absent.

tasks.title: Security settings screen
tasks.what: Settings screen sections for the blocked-sites list and per-site permissions: view, allow, revoke.
tasks.why: Without a screen you would have to edit files to block a site or revoke a camera grant. If websites could reach these commands, they could unblock themselves.
tasks.how: Add them to the P3 settings screen, saving only through checked app commands. A test adds a block and a camera grant, restarts, and checks both are kept and enforced.
tasks.chain: You manage blocked sites and permissions → add them to the settings screen through checked app commands → websites still cannot touch them.
tasks.check: A block and a grant persist after restart and are enforced; revoking works; websites cannot call these commands.

tasks.title: Design the cost experiments
tasks.what: Small timing tests for the rules engine and permission checks, plus finished designs for the two security-cost experiments.
tasks.why: Measuring without a design written first invites picking the numbers that look best. P6 needs the plan ready and approved before any campaign runs.
tasks.how: Write small timing tests for the rules engine and permission checks, and finish both experiment pages with their workloads, measures and analysis plan.
tasks.chain: Security costs time and memory → build small timing tests and finish the experiment designs, claiming no numbers → P6 measures it properly.
tasks.check: Small timing tests run (proof the tool works, not results); experiment pages updated; you approve them.

tasks.title: Literature batch 4
tasks.what: A batch of reading on site isolation, embedded-browser security and WebView security studies.
tasks.why: Without this reading the paper could present known trade-offs as new, or miss attacks others have already described.
tasks.how: Read studies on site isolation and embedded-browser and WebView security, and write one dated note per source.
tasks.chain: The paper needs security context → read site-isolation and embedded-browser security studies → the trade-offs are grounded.

tasks.title: Gate and your review
tasks.what: The phase gate and your review, including the threat model.
tasks.why: Some risks are left open on purpose. You should know which ones before calling P4 done, because they affect how safely you can use Ferrum.
tasks.how: Run the gate and save all evidence. You review the threat model and the 'not enforced' list, do the hand checks and approve.
tasks.chain: Controls are tested → run the gate → you review the threat model and the 'not enforced' list, and approve.
tasks.check: All evidence saved; wiki clean; you approved the P4 exit.

test_gate.explanation: Security claims need proof → attack-style tests try the known bypasses, every rule branch is covered, and the release build is scanned → you accept the 'not enforced' list → only then does P5 start.

rows.proves: Dependencies are allowed and have no open alerts.
Every rules-engine decision branch is tested.
Each of the ten security items has a passing test.
P2 and P3 suites and the bridge lockdown still pass.
Shell style, types and tests pass.
The app you would ship builds.
The release build cannot skip security.
Each mode separates what it should.
You read the threat model, blocked a site, and saw a camera or location request denied.
